title: Bearnaise Sauce
subtitle: tarragon and shallot butter sauce
excerpt: Bearnaise is a variation of hollandaise, flavoured with a reduction of tarragon, shallots, and vinegar. It is the classic sauce for steak. The method is the same as hollandaise but the reduction gives it a more complex, herby character.
sourceNotes: Bearnaise sauce was created in 1837 at the restaurant Le Pavillon Henri IV near Paris. It takes its name from the Bearn region of France, home of King Henry IV.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make just before serving. Keep warm over hot water for up to 45 minutes.

content.text: The reduction must cool before you add the egg yolks. If it is too hot it will cook the eggs as soon as they go in. Reduce to about 2 tablespoons of liquid.
Put the shallots, tarragon stalks, vinegar, and peppercorns in a small saucepan. Reduce over medium heat until you have about 2 tablespoons of liquid. Strain and cool.
Put the egg yolks and cooled reduction in a heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water.
Whisk constantly until thick, pale, and ribbon-like. Remove from the heat.
Slowly whisk in the warm melted butter, a little at a time, until all is incorporated.
Stir in the fresh tarragon leaves. Season with salt. Serve immediately with steak or fish.

items.cause: Butter added too fast or heat too high
items.fix: Whisk a fresh egg yolk in a clean bowl and slowly add the split sauce, drop by drop.

items.cause: Fresh tarragon leaves not added at the end
items.fix: Add more finely chopped fresh tarragon leaves when finishing the sauce.

content.text: Bearnaise was created in 1837 at Le Pavillon Henri IV near Paris. It is now the defining sauce for steak in French cuisine. The use of tarragon distinguishes it clearly from hollandaise -- the anise note of the herb pairs well with the charred, savoury flavour of grilled meat. It is also served with fish and vegetables across France.
